title: Reducer and context boundary

sources.locator: React Learn and Reference; React 19.2; provisions applicable to Reducer and context boundary
sources.claim: Reducer plus context can share state and dispatch across a bounded subtree without threading every prop.

canonicalExplanation.summary: When many components deep in one feature need the same state and actions, passing props through every layer gets noisy ("prop drilling"). **Context** lets a parent **provide** a value and any descendant **read** it with `useContext`. Pair it with a reducer: provide `state` and `dispatch` from one **provider component** placed at the top of the **feature's subtree**, not the whole app. Split rarely-changing values (dispatch, services) from often-changing state into separate contexts, and wrap them in small hooks like `useEditorState()` that throw a clear error when used outside the provider.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A course editor has a sidebar, a lesson list, a lesson form and a preview. The editor state is passed as props through four layers that don't use it. Someone suggests putting all app state into one global context. A course editor provides state and dispatch only to its editing subtree and splits stable services from changing data. In this lesson you'll design and test a provider boundary for a multi-component feature.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **State and events** module, **Forms and native controls**, **useReducer**, and **Component API design**, because the provider and hooks form the feature's public interface.

examples.title: The course editor's provider
examples.situation: A course editor provides state and dispatch only to its editing subtree and splits stable services from changing data.
walkthrough: **Bound the feature:** CourseEditorProvider wraps Sidebar, LessonForm and Preview, and nothing else.
**Split contexts:** dispatch goes in its own stable context, while state goes in another, so buttons that only dispatch don't re-render.
**Test:** a test will render LessonForm inside the provider, type a title, and check Preview shows it; rendering outside will throw the clear error.
examples.result: Editor components talk through one boundary without prop drilling, and the rest of the app is unaffected.

examples.title: The context that re-rendered the whole app
examples.situation: A team puts user, theme, cart and editor state in one AppContext at the root. Typing in the lesson form re-renders the header, footer and every page.
walkthrough: Every consumer of AppContext re-renders when any part of its value changes.
Editor state changes on each keystroke.
Fix: move editor state into CourseEditorProvider around the editor only, and split unrelated contexts.
examples.result: Typing re-renders only editor components, and the header stays still.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Context should replace all props and local state throughout an application.
misconceptions.correction: Context is for values many components in a subtree need. Ordinary props are clearer for direct parent-child data, local state stays local, and one giant context re-renders every consumer on any change.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The context that re-rendered the whole app", what caused the extra re-renders?

analogy.example: A provider is like **the Wi-Fi in one office**. Anyone in that office can connect without running a cable from the router to each desk (prop drilling). You don't broadcast one office's network across the whole building, and the guest network (dispatch) is kept separate from the busy one (state).
limitations: Wi-Fi doesn't re-render desks; context changes do re-render consumers.
A desk next to the router still uses a cable: short props are fine.

steps.explanation: The course editor provides state and dispatch only to its editing subtree.

nearTransfer.prompt: Create a `QuizProvider` around a quiz page with separate state and dispatch contexts and `useQuiz()` / `useQuizDispatch()` hooks that throw outside the provider.

farTransfer.prompt: Refactor a feature that drills props through 3+ levels into a reducer + context boundary. Write tests for: a consumer updating state, another consumer seeing it, and the hook error outside the provider.
scaffold: Keep the boundary as small as possible.
Keep direct props where they're clearer.

remediation.explanation: Before adding context ask: **Which components need this, and what's their closest shared parent?** Put the provider there, not at the root. **Does anything only dispatch?** Give dispatch its own context.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The context that re-rendered the whole app".

recap.summary: To design and test a provider boundary for a multi-component feature, keep state in a reducer, provide state and dispatch in separate contexts from a provider around just that feature's subtree, expose them through hooks with clear errors, and keep ordinary props and local state where they're simpler.
